title: Mahn v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)
frame:
Forum: Federal Court.
Parties as styled: applicant = PRINCE JUTY MAHN; respondent = THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board, which upheld the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The judge is the author (layer 1). The applicant and respondent in this proceeding make submissions to the judge (layer 2). The decision under review was made by an earlier decision-maker (layer 3), and that decision may itself report what a claimant, the Minister or a witness said to that decision-maker (layer 4).

paragraphs.text: The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board, which upheld the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

The Applicant has not established that the RAD made a reviewable error in confirming the rejection of his claim on credibility grounds. The RAD also reasonably refused to admit his proposed new evidence. Accordingly, this application for judicial review is dismissed.
On August 23, 2023, the Applicant arrived in Canada on a visitor visa and, on November 3, 2023, claimed refugee protection.
The Applicant’s refugee claim is based on an alleged fear of harm in Liberia at the hands of traditional elders and the Chief Zoe of the Gayelahdee clan.

In his Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative, the Applicant alleged being an ordained Christian minister. In December 2022, he and his wife traveled from Monrovia to his hometown to visit his ailing father. The Chief Zoe and elders demanded that, as the first male child, he take over his father’s ancestral role as “country devil”. The Applicant refused because of his Christian faith. Following threats against their lives, the Applicant and his wife returned to Monrovia.

In August 2023, the Applicant traveled to Canada on a visitor visa to attend a pastoral church conference. He alleged that, on October 9, 2023, a group of elders and Chief Zoes showed up at his family residence in Monrovia, threatening to kidnap his wife and children. The Applicant’s wife contacted a pastor friend, Pastor James, who arrived with police officers to rescue the family and take them into hiding.

On October 24, 2024, the RPD rejected the claim, holding that the Applicant was neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, as he failed to adduce sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence to establish his claim.
On November 3, 2024, represented by new counsel, the Applicant appealed the RPD’s decision before the RAD.

On April 3, 2025, the RAD dismissed the appeal and confirmed the RPD’s decision, holding that the Applicant “is not credible regarding the central allegations of his claim”. Specifically, its findings were as follows: a)The RAD refused to admit three new affidavits sought to be adduced by the Applicant, from his “half-brother”, his uncle, and his mother. Although the affidavits were signed after the RPD decision, they described events that occurred before the RPD hearing and could have been submitted earlier with due diligence; b)Even if the RAD admitted the affidavits as new evidence, it would still not have found them credible given their source. Also, the affiants did not provide copies of identity cards, leaving the panel unable to verify their identities on a balance of probabilities; c)The RPD erred in concluding, on one hand, that “there is no credible evidence relevant to [the Applicant’s] claim”, while accepting, on the other hand, that he was approached in his village to take over his father’s role as a traditional leader. However, this error was not “serious enough to undermine the overall correctness of [the RPD’s] decision”, as the Applicant is not credible with respect to central allegations of his claim; d)Conducting its own review, the RAD found that the Applicant failed to establish that he is the only one to whom the position of “country devil” can be transmitted and that his brother Jeremiah would not be similarly targeted because he is his half-brother on his mother’s side. In his BOC form, he omitted to mention that Jeremiah was a half-brother. He also did not persuade the RAD that his Jeremiah was carrying the Mahn family name “simply because he chose to do so”; e)Additionally, the RAD drew a negative credibility inference because the Applicant’s oral testimony, in which he claimed he was chosen because he is his father’s only biological male child, contradicted his statement in his BOC narrative that he was chosen for being the “first male child”, a claim further undermined by his oral admission that his brother Jeremiah is older than he is; f)The RAD drew a further negative credibility inference from the Applicant’s failure to provide evidence on the circumstances of his brother Jeremiah or why he was not targeted, rejecting his explanation that he was no longer in touch with him, because the Applicant had successfully maintained contact with other family members and obtained documents from Liberia; g)The RAD held that a news article featuring a photo of a masked “country devil” in Gbarpolu County could not be reliably linked to the Applicant’s father in Nimba County; h)The RAD further did not accept the Applicant’s testimony on how the elders found his Monrovia home. Despite testifying at the hearing that his uncle led the traditional elders to his Monrovia residence, the Applicant failed to mention his uncle in his BOC narrative; i)The RAD assigned low probative value to an October 9, 2023, email and a July 2, 2024, letter purportedly from the Applicant’s wife. The email referred to harassment, but not to any threat to kidnap her and the children, which was first alleged in the later letter. Further, the RAD drew a negative inference from the fact that the letter appeared to have been written by a third party, rather than by the Applicant’s wife; j)The RAD found a police report not genuine on a balance of probabilities, noting for instance that a key passage mirrored the exact phrasing of a support letter from the Global Revival Center and that it was not drafted as a genuine investigation into the Applicant’s allegations; k)The RAD gave low probative value to a letter from a church leader, because its similarity to the police report undermined its authenticity and it lacked clear evidence of how the authors knew about the events; l)The RAD was of the view that National Documentation Package reports on Liberia did not establish that secret societies abduct or mistreat individuals in Monrovia for forced initiation; m)Finally, the RAD rejected the Applicant’s arguments that the RPD failed to consider his cultural background and alleged trauma associated with his refusal to assume the role of the “country devil” and that the RPD misapplied the legal tests for persecution and state protection.

This application for judicial review raises the following two issues: a)Was it unreasonable for the Refugee Appeal Division to refuse to admit the Applicant’s proposed new evidence? b)Was it unreasonable for the Refugee Appeal Division to dismiss the Applicant’s appeal and confirm the RPD’s rejection of the Applicant’s refugee claim based on his absence of credibility? IV. Analysis A. Standard of review

This Court applies the reasonableness standard of review when reviewing the merits of a RAD decision. This includes the RAD’s conclusions related to a claimant’s credibility (Bamidele v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2026 FC 999 at para 15) and the admission of new evidence on appeal (Bhuiyan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2026 FC 616 at para 50).

In applying the reasonableness standard of review, the role of a reviewing court is to examine the reasons given by the administrative decision maker and to determine whether the decision is based on “an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis” and is “justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 85 [Vavilov]).

When assessing a decision on judicial review, the Court must determine whether the decision at issue bears the hallmarks of reasonableness, namely justification, transparency and intelligibility (Vavilov at para 99). Any flaws relied upon by the party challenging the decision must be “sufficiently central or significant to render the decision unreasonable” (Vavilov at para 100).
For the following reasons, I am not convinced the RAD made any reviewable error in refusing to admit the Applicant’s proposed new evidence.
paragraphs.heading_before: B. The RAD’s conclusions on the Applicant’s proposed new evidence

paragraphs.text: The onus was on the Applicant to establish that the proposed new evidence was admissible pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA), which requires an appellant to show that (i) the evidence arose after the RPD decision; or (ii) the evidence was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (iii) the appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented it to the RPD at the time of the decision (Figueroa v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 521 at para 19).

The RAD is strictly bound to apply the test set out in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and has no discretion to disregard the explicit criteria set out therein (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Singh, 2016 FCA 96 at para 63 [Singh]).

In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal further held that the Raza criteria, developed for pre-removal risk assessments, also apply to subsection 110(4) of the IRPA. Accordingly, before admitting evidence under subsection 110(4), the RAD must also assess its credibility, relevance, newness and materiality (Raza v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 at para 13; Singh at para 49).

A claimant is required to put their best foot forward before the RPD and present all the evidence that is available at the time (Thuraisingam v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 1332 at para 10; Abdullahi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 260 at para 14). This means that a claimant is not entitled to submit new evidence “every time he or she is surprised by the RPD’s decision” (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Desalegn, 2016 FC 12 at para 23).

Thus, evidence that simply “corroborates facts, contradicts the RPD’s findings, or clarifies the evidence before the RPD”, does not qualify as “new evidence” under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA (Singh at para 50). Put simply, it is not the role of the RAD “to provide the opportunity to complete a deficient record submitted before the RPD” (Singh at para 54).

In the case at bar, the RAD reasonably concluded that the documents sought to be adduced by the Applicant did not meet the test for admission of new evidence on appeal under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

While the RAD did not dispute that the Applicant’s proposed new affidavits post-dated the RPD decision, it noted the allegations in these affidavits pertained to events that took place before the RPD decision. However, as the RAD noted, the Applicant “[…] did not explain on appeal why these exhibits were not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or why the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring them to the RPD before the decision” (RAD reasons at para 11). Indeed, in the present case, the Applicant had a three-month window between the hearing and the issuance of the RPD’s decision to obtain and submit corroborating evidence if he wished to do so.

The RAD reasonably rejected the Applicant’s argument that the documents “arose as a direct response to the RPD’s findings” and could not, for this reason, have been presented earlier. As noted by the RAD, the documents seek to address issues that the RPD expressly canvassed the hearing as raising credibility concerns (RAD reasons at para 11).

The Applicant argues that, while the RPD Member indicated at the hearing that the role of his uncle and the news article photograph raised credibility issues, the Member did not signal any skepticism regarding Jeremiah’s status as “half-brother”. He therefore justifies the admission of the proposed affidavit from his “half-brother” on the basis that the RPD’s credibility concerns could not have been reasonably anticipated.

I disagree. The Member did ask the Applicant why Jeremiah would carry his father’s name if he was his half-brother. This is when the Applicant said that this was Jeremiah’s choice (Transcript of RPD hearing at page 16). The Member also asked why his brother could not assume the function of “country devil”, to which the Applicant answered that such role can only be passed on to the biological child (Transcript of RPD hearing at page 36). In my view, these lines of questioning from the Member clearly put the Applicant on notice that Jeremiah’s lineage and ineligibility to become “country devil” were live issues.

It is trite that credibility is always in issue in refugee hearings (Talukder v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 668 at para 20). Importantly, the RPD’s credibility concerns arose directly from the material discrepancies and omissions in the Applicant’s own BOC narrative and oral testimony. The Applicant therefore cannot reasonably argue that the RPD’s credibility findings could not have been anticipated.
As such, I find nothing unreasonable in how the RAD evaluated and chose to exclude the Applicant’s proposed affidavits.

The foregoing suffices to dispose of the Applicant’s arguments on the admissibility of his purported new evidence under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA. As such, I do not need to address his alternative argument challenging the RAD’s finding that the affidavits failed to satisfy the Raza factors (RAD reasons at para 12).

For the following reasons, I am also of the view that the RAD acted reasonably in confirming the RPD’s finding that the Applicant was not credible regarding the central allegations of his claim (RAD reasons at paras 14, 17, 19 and 54).
paragraphs.heading_before: C. The RAD’s conclusion on the Applicant’s credibility

paragraphs.text: The RAD highlighted several credibility problems, including various inconsistencies and omissions, arising from the Applicant’s BOC narrative and oral testimony. These problems pertained to the central allegations put forward by the Applicant in support of his claim (RAD reasons at paras 18-32).
Further, the RAD assigned low probative value to the documentary evidence the Applicant submitted as part of his claim (RAD reasons at paras 33-46).

Finally, the RAD concluded that the objective evidence contained in the National Documentation Package related to Liberia did not support the Applicant’s alleged risk of abduction and mistreatment in Monrovia (RAD reasons at paras 47-49).
I now address each of these points in turn.

The RAD’s credibility analysis focused on three key aspects of the Applicant’s claim: first, his claim that, even though he has a brother, the position of “country devil” can be passed on only to him; second, his attempt to link an unidentifiable, masked figure in a published news article to his father; and third, his assertion that his uncle directed the pursuers to his home in Monrovia.
paragraphs.heading_before: 1. Credibility problems affecting the Applicant’s central allegations

paragraphs.text: On the first central point, the Applicant alleged that his brother Jeremiah was his “half-brother” on the maternal side. For this reason, he was not eligible to succeed his father as “country devil” and, as such, he would not be similarly targeted by traditionalists, even though he has remained in Liberia (RAD reasons at para 21).

The RAD reasonably determined that the Applicant failed to establish with sufficient and persuasive evidence the status of Jeremiah as his “half-brother”. The following elements suffice to establish the reasonableness of the RAD’s conclusion on this point.

As the RAD pointed out, in his BOC form, the applicant listed Jeremiah as his “brother” and they share the same last name as the Applicant’s father, Mahn. Nowhere in the BOC form did the applicant refer to Jeremiah as his “half-brother”, despite being instructed to indicate the relationship he had with each family member, “including half-brothers and half-sisters” (RAD reasons at para 24).

As well, the RAD also reasonably observed that the applicant referred to himself as his father’s “only biological male child” during oral testimony, whereas he referred to himself as the “first” male child in the BOC form, a claim further undermined by his oral admission that his brother is older than he is (RAD reasons at para 26).

Further, the RAD could reasonably agree with the RPD’s decision to draw a negative credibility inference from the Applicant’s failure to provide any evidence on the circumstances of his brother Jeremiah or why he was not targeted by the elders. While the Applicant affirmed he was no longer in touch with him, the Applicant successfully maintained contact with other family members and obtained documents from Liberia (RAD reasons at para 28).

While a presumption of truthfulness attaches to a claimant’s testimony (Maldonado v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1980] 2 FC 302 at 305 [Maldonado]), and claimants are generally not required to provide corroborating evidence (Senadheerage v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 968 at para 27 [Senadheerage]), the RAD can draw a negative credibility inference based on the claimant’s lack of effort to obtain corroborative evidence, when there is already a valid reason to question a claimant’s credibility, such evidence could reasonably be expected to be available, and there is no reasonable explanation for its absence (Senadheerage at para 36; Lawani at para 25).

On the second central issue underlying the claim, the RAD reasonably rejected the Applicant’s assertion that his father was represented in a news article showing a picture of a masked, unidentifiable figure. The Applicant did not submit any independent, objective evidence establishing that the person in the picture was indeed his father. Moreover, the article concerned an event in a different county from the one where his father allegedly served as “country devil” (RAD reasons at para 29).

The RAD also reasonably concluded that the Applicant’s testimony regarding how the photograph was obtained lacked plausibility. It was indeed improbable that his wife, living in strict concealment in Monrovia due to her fear of Nimba traditionalists, would invite a stranger from Nimba into her safe house merely to hand-deliver a publicly accessible photograph (RAD reasons at para 30). The RAD may draw conclusions concerning an appellant’s credibility based on implausibilities, common sense and rationality (Lawani v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 924 at para 26 [Lawani]).

Finally, on the third central issue, the RAD reasonably dismissed the Applicant’s belated testimony about his uncle. In his BOC narrative, the Applicant omitted any mention of his uncle, stating simply that the elders and Chief Zoes paid a visit to his Monrovia residence. However, when pressed at the hearing to explain how pursuers from a remote village could locate his family’s specific address in a metropolitan city like Monrovia, the Applicant testified for the first time that his uncle had led the elders to his home (RAD reasons at para 32).

Given that the uncle’s alleged betrayal was the critical link that facilitated the very visit triggering the Applicant’s refugee claim, the RAD acted reasonably in concluding that the Applicant amended his story in order to resolve a gap in his narrative.

In conclusion on this point, I note the Applicant also submits that the RAD erred in stating that the RPD had found his claim to be “manifestly unfounded” (RAD reasons at para 15). However, as his counsel properly conceded at the hearing, this error is not determinative. Because the RAD conducted a full, independent assessment of the merits, the Applicant suffered no prejudice, and this oversight alone does not vitiate the RAD’s decision.
For the following reasons, I am also of the view that the RAD reasonably assessed the documentary evidence submitted by the Applicant in support of his claim.
paragraphs.heading_before: 2. The sufficiency of the Applicant’s documentary evidence

paragraphs.text: Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the RAD is mandated to base its decisions on evidence considered “credible or trustworthy in the circumstances” (subsection 171(a.3) of the IRPA). In the present case, there were numerous problems that undermined the weight to be given to the Applicant’s materials.

First, the RAD reasonably concluded that the written communications from the Applicant’s wife carried low probative value (RAD reasons at paras 36-37). The email of October 9, 2023, which was sent the exact day the agents of persecution visited the family home, completely omitted any reference to a threat of kidnapping.

The RAD could reasonably find it implausible that the Applicant’s wife would omit a threat as central and severe as the abduction of her children. This critical allegation only surfaced months later in her subsequent letter of July 2, 2024. Further, even though it was supposedly written by the Applicant’s wife, the letter referred to her in the third person (“his wife and children”), legitimately casting doubt on whether she was indeed the letter’s true author.

Also, the RAD acted reasonably in concluding, on a balance of probabilities, that the investigation report from the Office of the Special Investigations Unit was not a genuine document. A key passage in this official report closely mirrored the wording of a separate letter from the Global Revival Center. The RAD was justified in drawing a negative inference regarding the authenticity of the report based on this identical wording. Further, the RAD could draw a negative inference from the fact that the report is a written in a way that concludes that the police cannot do anything about the threats faced by the Applicant. Indeed, the report concludes with a “recommendation” that the Applicant’s wife and children remain in hiding, and that the Applicant seek refugee, while the police complete its investigation (RAD reasons at paras 40-41).

Similarly, I find no reviewable error in the RAD’s assessment of the support letter from the Global Revival Center (RAD reasons at paras 45-46). The RAD reasonably chose to assign the document low probative value because it contained language that was similar to that found in the police report, undermining its authenticity. Also, the letter did not indicate how its authors, who are church administrators located in Monrovia, obtained knowledge of the specific threats made against the Applicant on October 9, 2023 (whether they witnessed it or were simply told by the Applicant about it).

Finally, the RAD reasonably determined that the Applicant’s allegations of forward-looking risk in Monrovia were not supported by the objective evidence on country conditions set out in the National Documentation Package regarding Liberia (RAD reasons at paras 47-49).
paragraphs.heading_before: 3. The assessment of the objective evidence on country conditions

paragraphs.text: As the RAD noted, while the UN Mission in Liberia report documents instances of Poro society members forcefully initiating individuals who transgress traditional rules, it does not document any instances of abduction or mistreatment occurring in the capital city of Monrovia (RAD reasons at para 47). The RAD also noted that the objective documentation submitted by the Applicant himself confirmed that the issue is predominantly one of rural communities, given that the article reported that a trial was transferred from a rural county to Monrovia to avoid juror bias (RAD reasons at para 49).
In conclusion, having regard to the totality of the evidence in the record, I am satisfied that the RAD’s decision was reasonable. The outcome is supported by reasons which are logical and rational.
paragraphs.heading_before: D. Applicant’s argument on the “presumption of credibility”

paragraphs.text: As such, it was reasonably open to the RAD to conclude that the RPD was correct that the Appellant is not credible regarding the central allegations to his claim and, on that basis, dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

I note that the Applicant devoted a substantial portion of both his written and oral arguments to the position that the RAD failed to apply the “presumption of credibility” and made no explicit finding that it was rebutted.

In my view, this argument has no merit. The RAD explicitly addressed this issue when it indicated it disagreed with the Applicant’s argument that “[…] the RPD relied in its findings on minor inconsistencies and speculations before deciding that the presumption of truthfulness has been rebutted” (RAD reasons at para 20).

More importantly, the presumption of truthfulness is rebutted when a claimant’s credibility is fundamentally undermined by inconsistencies and omissions in both their BOC narrative and oral testimony, without the necessity for the RAD to explicitly state that the presumption has been displaced (Maldonado at page 305; Zerihaymanot v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 610 at para 41).
For these reasons, I dismiss the application for judicial review.

Neither party proposed a serious question of general importance for certification. I am satisfied that none arises. JUDGMENT IN IMM-9550-25 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that The application for judicial review is dismissed.
